title: MICrONS neurons kept their movie responses across scans up to four sessions apart; coupling, input counts and connections did not predict the small changes in 1,015 manually matched neurons
abstract: We asked if the wiring of a cortical neuron predicts how stable its visual responses are across imaging scans. We used one MICrONS mouse (17797): oracle movie responses (6 clips, 6 to 10 repeats) in 8 scans from 5 sessions, same-neuron matches from the manual (primary) and automatic coregistration tables, and EM input counts and connections. For each neuron in two scans we calculated a noise-corrected signal correlation (rho). Responses were stable: the median rho was 0.94 for the same neuron and 0.18 for the nearest other neuron, 0.95 for scans in one session and 0.94 for scans 1 to 4 sessions apart; scan-pair differences were larger than gap effects. In 1,015 manually matched neurons, population coupling (slope +0.023 SD per SD, 95% CI -0.041 to 0.090), log input synapses, inhibitory input fraction and soma, spine and shaft input counts did not clearly predict stability. The coupling result does not support the prediction of Sweeney and Clopath (2020) that coupled neurons drift more; in 4,841 automatically matched neurons the slope was +0.043 (0.015 to 0.071). Automatic matches also gave positive input-count and inhibitory-fraction slopes, but a post hoc check put them in the low-rho tail that includes coregistration errors. EM-connected pairs did not change their responses together more than matched unconnected pairs (automatic, 15,240 connected pairs: -0.003, CI -0.0046 to -0.0015). Limitations: one mouse, ordinal session gaps, imaging-plane differences between scans, unproofread EM connections.
